summary: Defines MIB objects for managing traffic engineering with Generalized MPLS, letting operators configure and monitor GMPLS-based tunnels through network management protocols.

eli5.summary: This is a control panel for GMPLS paths. A network operator can read and set values to see and shape the routes that traffic follows.

subtitle: The management tables that let operators configure and monitor GMPLS traffic-engineered tunnels over SNMP.

tldr.problem: Operators needed a standard way to set up and watch GMPLS traffic-engineered tunnels, which add things like bidirectional paths, link protection and non-packet labels that the MPLS TE MIB does not cover.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4802 defines the GMPLS-TE-STD-MIB module, which extends the MPLS-TE-STD-MIB of RFC 3812 with tables for tunnel settings, hop lists, per-tunnel errors and reverse-direction counters, plus a new gmplsTunnelDown notification.
tldr.outcome: A router can be managed over SNMP with the same tunnel model for MPLS and GMPLS, and an MPLS TE implementation can migrate by adding the new tables and objects. It is a companion to RFC 4803.

today: RFC 4802 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2007, and no RFC in the unit metadata obsoletes or updates it. It is used together with RFC 4803.

sections.title: Introduction and Migration Strategy
sections.content:
RFC 4802 defines a MIB (Management Information Base) module for Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS) traffic engineering (TE). Network management software normally reaches a MIB through SNMP. The tables here extend those that RFC 3812 defined for MPLS traffic engineering, so managing GMPLS TE is built on managing MPLS TE. The RFC says it should be used together with the companion document RFC 4803.

The module, named GMPLS-TE-STD-MIB, extends the MPLS one through augmentations and sparse augmentations of its tables. The only additions are for GMPLS or for the greater complexity of MPLS and GMPLS systems. To migrate, an implementation only has to add the new tables and objects.

Setting gmplsTunnelLSPEncoding to tunnelLspNotGmpls lets a plain MPLS-TE tunnel use the extra objects without running the GMPLS protocols.
sections.eli5: It is like adding a new set of buttons to a remote control you already have. The old buttons still work, and the new ones handle the fancier features.

sections.title: Tunnels, Segments and the Framework
sections.content:
The RFC calls an explicitly routed LSP (ERLSP) a GMPLS tunnel. At the ingress and egress LSRs it consists of in-segments and/or out-segments, each tied to one GMPLS-enabled interface. At an intermediate LSR a connection is one or more in-segments and/or out-segments, joined by a cross-connect. These segment objects live in the MPLS LSR MIB of RFC 3813, with GMPLS extensions in RFC 4803.

The module follows the Internet-Standard Management Framework. Objects are defined with SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579, RFC 2580) and are generally read and written through SNMP.

Only point-to-point tunnel segments are supported, although multipoint-to-point and point-to-multipoint connections can be built by an LSR acting as a cross-connect. Each tunnel has at most one out-segment originating at an LSR and/or one in-segment terminating there.
sections.eli5: A tunnel is a road made of short stretches joined at junctions. This document describes how to write down each stretch and junction in a form a computer can manage.

sections.title: The GMPLS TE Tables
sections.content:
Setting up GMPLS tunnels takes three kinds of configuration: MPLS parameters from RFC 3812, GMPLS parameters on top of them, and loose or strict source-routed hops. The new tables cover the GMPLS part.

  • gmplsTunnelTable sparsely extends the MPLS tunnel table so GMPLS tunnels can be created, reconfigured or removed. Three of its objects use enumerations from signaling, kept in textual conventions maintained by IANA so the MIB does not need to change when signaling gains new values.
  • gmplsTunnelHopTable holds extra parameters for the strict or loose hops of a signaled tunnel. Several tunnels may share hops by pointing at the same entry.
  • gmplsTunnelARHopTable lists the actual hops the tunnel took, as reported by signaling after setup. Support is optional.
  • gmplsTunnelCHopTable lists hops computed by a constraint-based routing algorithm from the hop table. Support is optional.
  • gmplsTunnelErrorTable records the last error on each tunnel: its nature, when and how it was reported, and recovery advice in an admin string.
  • gmplsTunnelReversePerfTable adds counters for bidirectional tunnels in which packets are visible.

The tables support both manually configured and signaled tunnels.
sections.eli5: There is one big form for each tunnel and several smaller forms for its stops, the route it really took, its last problem and its traffic counts.

sections.title: Key Tunnel Settings
sections.content:
The main gmplsTunnelTable adds the GMPLS-specific choices for each tunnel:

  • gmplsTunnelLSPEncoding is the encoding of the requested LSP; tunnelLspNotGmpls (the default) means GMPLS signaling is not in use.
  • gmplsTunnelSwitchingType selects the switching on links that advertise more than one type.
  • gmplsTunnelGPid says what payload the LSP carries.
  • gmplsTunnelLinkProtection is a bitmask of the protection wanted: extraTraffic, unprotected, shared, dedicatedOneToOne, dedicatedOnePlusOne and enhanced. Zero bits means any protection may be used.
  • gmplsTunnelDirection is forward (the default) or bidirectional.
  • gmplsTunnelPathComp tells the source how to compute the path: dynamicFull, explicit or dynamicPartial.
  • gmplsTunnelSecondary marks a secondary LSP, and gmplsTunnelAttributes can request label recording.

The table also holds notification-recipient addresses and gmplsTunnelAdminStatusFlags.
sections.eli5: These are the choices on the tunnel form: what kind of road, what it carries, how much backup it gets, whether traffic goes one way or both, and who plans the route.

sections.title: Labels, Counters, Errors and Notifications
sections.content:
Labels. The hop tables and the segment tables of RFC 3813 have objects of syntax MplsLabel, a 32-bit integer. Some GMPLS labels are longer, are built from sub-fields, or are concatenated. So each such object has a companion row pointer. If the pointer is zeroDotZero (0.0), the label is the 32-bit integer; otherwise the pointer names a row elsewhere, such as in the gmplsLabelTable of RFC 4803.

Counters. 64-bit counters exist for fast interfaces, following the rule copied from RFC 2863: at 20,000,000 bits per second or less, 32-bit counters must be supported; above that and below 650,000,000, 32-bit packet counters and 64-bit octet counters; at 650,000,000 or faster, 64-bit for both.

Failure reporting. The gmplsTunnelDown notification replaces mplsTunnelDown for GMPLS tunnels and also reports the cause. An implementation must not issue both for the same event.
sections.eli5: Some labels are too big for the little box on the old form, so the form points to a bigger box. When a tunnel breaks, the new alarm also says why.

sections.title: Worked Example: Setting Up a Tunnel
sections.content:
The RFC walks through creating a best effort, loosely routed, bidirectional TE tunnel over two hops. It uses a Generalized Label request with Lambda encoding, label recording and shared link layer protection, and all objects are created on the head-end LSR.

The steps are: create the mplsTunnelTable row with createAndWait(5); add the gmplsTunnelTable row (tunnelLspLambda, lsc, shared(2), bidirectional(1)); create a resource row and two hop rows (the first strict, the second loose); add a gmplsLabelTable row and a gmplsTunnelHopTable row pointing to it for the first hop; activate the first hop; and finally set the tunnel row to active(1). The second hop needs no GMPLS hop entry because it has no special GMPLS features.
sections.eli5: The example is a recipe: fill in the tunnel form, list the stops, attach the special label, then switch the whole thing on last so nothing starts half-ready.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Objects with read-write or read-create access can be dangerous in an insecure environment. The gmplsTunnelTable and gmplsTunnelHopTable provision tunnels at their ingress LSRs, so unauthorized writes could disrupt traffic, especially for a tunnel that is already established.

Reading is sensitive too: the tunnel, hop, actual-hop, computed-hop, reverse-performance and error tables reveal the tunnel topology and status. SNMP versions before SNMPv3 lacked adequate security. The RFC recommends SNMPv3 with its cryptographic authentication and privacy, says deploying earlier SNMP versions is NOT RECOMMENDED, and makes the operator responsible for granting access only to legitimate principals.
sections.eli5: Whoever holds the control panel can change or peek at the roads, so only trusted people should get a key, and the key should be hard to copy.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA rooted GMPLS-TE-STD-MIB under the mplsStdMIB subtree as number 13 (1.3.6.1.2.1.10.166). Future GMPLS-related standards-track MIB modules should also go under that subtree, with new assignments only by Standards Action.

Three objects (gmplsTunnelLSPEncoding, gmplsTunnelSwitchingType and gmplsTunnelGPid) use textual conventions from the separate IANA-GMPLS-TC-MIB module, which IANA administers. Keeping it separate lets new values be added without reissuing this RFC.
sections.eli5: The numbers for the lists are handed out by a keeper of numbers, so new choices can be added later without rewriting the whole book.

viz.caption: THE SIX NEW TABLES IN GMPLS-TE-STD-MIB

items.title: gmplsTunnelHopTable
items.text: Extra parameters for strict or loose hops.

items.title: gmplsTunnelARHopTable
items.text: Actual hops reported by signaling. Optional.

items.title: gmplsTunnelCHopTable
items.text: Hops computed by constraint-based routing. Optional.

items.label: extraTraffic
items.desc: Use links protecting other traffic; may be preempted when that traffic's links fail.

items.label: unprotected
items.desc: Do not use any link layer protection.

items.label: shared
items.desc: Shared link layer protection such as 1:N.

items.label: enhanced
items.desc: A scheme more reliable than dedicated 1+1, for example 4 fiber BLSR/MS-SPRING.
